brave-llmcontext.snippet:
University of Houston physicists set a new ambient-pressure superconductivity record at 151 K, advancing research toward practical high-temperature superconductors.

University of Houston researchers achieved the highest ambient-pressure superconductivity temperature ever recorded, marking a major step toward practical high-temperature superconductors.
### Key Takeaways
- Researchers at the University of Houston and its Texas Center for Superconductivity set a new ambient-pressure superconductivity record of 151 K, the highest transition temperature achieved without maintaining high pressure since superconductivity was first discovered in 1911.
- The breakthrough uses a “pressure quenching” technique that locks in enhanced superconducting properties after pressure is removed, allowing the material to remain stable under normal conditions.
The UH team achieved a transition temperature (Tc) of 151 Kelvin (about minus 122 degrees Celsius) under ambient pressure — the highest ever recorded for all the reported superconductors at ambient pressure since the discovery of superconductivity in 1911. The transition temperature is the point below which a material becomes superconducting, meaning electricity can flow through it without resistance.
## Breaking the Temperature Barrier
This advance was made possible through a technique known as pressure quenching — a new approach for superconductors, though commonly used in other areas such as creating diamonds. In this method, researchers first apply intense pressure to the material to enhance its superconducting properties and raise its transition temperature.
While the material is under pressure, it is cooled to a specific temperature and rapidly released from pressure completely, effectively “locking in” the enhanced superconducting properties. Using this method, the researchers were able to preserve the higher Tc even after the pressure was removed, allowing the material to remain stable under normal conditions.

Intercalation is the reversible insertion of atoms, ions, or molecules into the galleries between layers of a layered material. It expands the interlayer spacing, weakens the van der Waals forces binding the layers together, and — crucially for this experiment — alters how strongly adjacent layers couple electronically. The Nobel Prize-winning chemistry behind lithium-ion batteries is built on precisely this process (lithium ions intercalating into layered cathode materials), though the organic intercalants used here are far larger molecules that dramatically expand the interlayer gap. By spacing the layers further apart, the organic intercalant caused 1T-TaS₂ to behave electronically as though it were much closer to the two-dimensional monolayer limit, while remaining mechanically robust enough to withstand the extreme pressures required to drive it into novel electronic territory. The crystal could then be studied at pressure regimes that would ordinarily destroy pristine samples. Two Paths to Superconductivity When the team compared the pressure-dependent phase diagrams of the intercalated and unmodified materials, the two diverged fundamentally. In the unmodified crystal, superconductivity appeared after the charge-density-wave state was suppressed, at a characteristic pressure — the familiar pathway documented in the field for more than a decade. In the organically-intercalated sample, however, superconductivity did not emerge at this same juncture. Instead, it appeared only at significantly higher pressures, and only after a different electronic ordered state had itself been suppressed. parallel.title: Evidence for spin-fluctuation-mediated superconductivity in electron-doped cuprates | Nature Physics
parallel.snippet:
Abstract

In conventional, phonon-mediated superconductors, the transition temperature and the linear-in-temperature normal-state scattering rate are linked through the electron–phonon coupling strength. In cuprate high-temperature superconductors, no equivalent relationship between critical temperature and electron–boson coupling has been identified. Here we highlight such a link with electrons scattering off commensurate antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations of variable strength. We use d.c. resistivity and high-field magnetoresistance to extract the scattering rate in electron-doped La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 as a function of doping. We reveal a highly anisotropic inelastic component to the scattering rate whose magnitude diminishes markedly as doping increases. The correlation we highlight between the strength of scattering and the critical temperature then identifies low-energy spin fluctuations as the primary pairing glue in electron-doped cuprates. The contrasting magnetotransport behaviour in hole-doped cuprates suggests that the higher critical temperature in those materials cannot be attributed solely to an increase in the coupling strength to the antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The success in modelling La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 reinforces the notion that resolving the origin of high-temperature superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates may require more than a simple extension of the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory.
